title: Online Auction
seoTitle: Design an Online Auction Platform Like eBay
description: Design an online auction system — listing items, placing bids with strong consistency, real-time bid updates and reliably closing auctions on time.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.text: Understanding the Problem

blocks.title: What is an Online Auction?
blocks.text: An online auction platform (like eBay) lets sellers list items with a starting price and end time, and lets buyers place bids. When the auction ends, the highest bidder wins.
Functional Requirements
Core Requirements

items: Users should be able to post an item for auction with a starting price and an end time.
Users should be able to bid on an item; a bid is accepted only if it is higher than the current highest bid.
Users should be able to view an auction, including the current highest bid, updated in real time.

blocks.text: Non-Functional Requirements
Core Requirements

items: Bidding must be strongly consistent — every user must agree on the current highest bid, and no accepted bid can be lost.
Bid updates should reach viewers in near real time (< 1s).
The system should handle popular auctions with thousands of concurrent bidders.
The system should scale to 10M concurrent auctions.

blocks.text: The Set Up
Planning the Approach

Bidding is a classic **contention** problem: many users racing to update the same value. We'll start simple and then focus deep dives on correctness under contention, real-time fan-out, and closing auctions.
Defining the Core Entities

items: **Item**: what's being sold — title, description, images.
**Auction**: an item listing with starting price, end time, status, and current max bid.
**Bid**: an amount placed by a user on an auction, with a timestamp and acceptance status.

blocks.text: API or System Interface

blocks.code:
POST /auctions
{ "item": {...}, "startingPrice": 100, "endTime": "2026-12-01T18:00:00Z" } -> Auction

POST /auctions/:auctionId/bids
{ "amount": 150 } -> Bid

GET /auctions/:auctionId -> Auction & Item

blocks.text: High-Level Design
1) Users should be able to post an item for auction
An **Auction Service** writes the Item and Auction rows. Images go to blob storage via presigned URLs, and the Auction stores references to them.
2) Users should be able to bid on an item
A **Bidding Service** handles bids. For every bid it reads the auction's current max, checks the new amount is higher, and writes the Bid while updating the max.
Done naively, two bids arriving together can both read the same max and both be accepted. We'll fix that in the first deep dive.
3) Users should be able to view an auction with real-time updates

Viewing an auction reads the Auction row (with its cached `maxBid`). To keep the price live, clients open a persistent connection and receive new highest bids as they happen — covered in the deep dives.
Potential Deep Dives
1) How do we guarantee bids are processed correctly under contention?

blocks.title: Pattern: Dealing with Contention
blocks.text: Many writers racing to change the same row is the heart of this pattern. The tools are atomic conditional updates, locks, or serialising writes through a single owner.

blocks.title: Read, check, then write in application code

approach.text: Read `maxBid`, compare in the service, then insert the bid and update the max as separate statements.

challenges.text: Classic race condition: two bids of 150 and 160 can both read max = 140 and both succeed, or a lower bid can overwrite a higher one.

blocks.title: Row lock with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE

approach.text: In one transaction, `SELECT max_bid FROM auctions WHERE id = ? FOR UPDATE`, compare, insert the bid, update `max_bid`, commit. Concurrent bidders on the same auction serialise on the row lock.

challenges.text: Correct, and fine for most auctions. For a very hot auction, bidders queue on the lock and latency grows; long-held locks also tie up connections.

approach.text: Skip the explicit lock and let the database compare-and-set in one statement:
If one row is updated, the bid wins and we insert it as accepted; if zero rows are updated, it lost and we record it as rejected. No lock is held across round trips.

challenges.text: Losing bids get a fast rejection, which is the desired behaviour. For extreme cases you can route all bids for one auction through a single partition of a queue (e.g. Kafka keyed by auctionId) so they are processed strictly in order by one consumer.

blocks.text: Always persist every bid — accepted or rejected — with its timestamp. Disputes ("I bid first!") are common, and an append-only bid log is your audit trail.
2) How do we push bid updates to viewers in real time?

challenges.text: Thousands of viewers per hot auction × one request per second is a lot of wasted load, and updates are still delayed by up to the poll interval.

approach.text: Viewers open an SSE connection to a **Notification Service**. When a bid is accepted, the Bidding Service publishes to a Redis Pub/Sub channel `auction:{id}`. Each notification server subscribes to the channels for the auctions its connected viewers are watching and pushes the new max to them.

challenges.text: Connections are stateful, so notification servers need connection-aware load balancing and clients must reconnect (SSE does this automatically) and re-fetch current state after a reconnect.

blocks.text: 3) How do we close auctions reliably and on time?
When `endTime` passes, the auction must stop accepting bids and a winner must be declared exactly once.

blocks.title: Cron job scanning for ended auctions

approach.text: Every minute, query `WHERE end_time <= now() AND status = 'OPEN'` and close them.

challenges.text: Up to a minute of slack where late bids could be accepted unless the bid query also checks `end_time`. Scanning gets heavier as data grows.

blocks.title: Delayed message + guard in the bid path

approach.text: When an auction is created, schedule a delayed message (e.g. SQS delay, a durable timer, or a job scheduler) for its end time. The consumer marks the auction `CLOSED` with a conditional update and emits a "winner" event. In the meantime, the bid's conditional update already includes `end_time > now()`, so no bid can sneak in after the deadline even if closing is delayed.

challenges.text: Clock skew between servers matters near the deadline; use the database's clock as the single source of truth. Closing must be idempotent in case the message is delivered twice.

blocks.text: Final Design

quiz.question: What prevents two concurrent bids from both being accepted against the same old max?
options: An atomic conditional UPDATE ... WHERE max_bid < :amount
quiz.explanation: The database evaluates the condition and writes atomically, so only one of the racing bids can win.

quiz.question: Why is SSE a good fit for live auction prices?
options: Viewers mostly receive updates; traffic is one-way from server to client
quiz.explanation: Bids go through normal HTTP requests; SSE efficiently pushes new prices down to many viewers.

quiz.question: How do you ensure no bid is accepted after the auction ends, even if closing is delayed?
options: Include end_time > now() in the bid's conditional update
quiz.explanation: The bid path itself enforces the deadline using the database clock.

quiz.question: Why record rejected bids too?
quiz.explanation: An append-only log of every bid and its outcome is the evidence when users dispute results.
